difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain: the argument links 'approved by the review board' and 'meets safety standards,' and concludes about funding. The student must supply the missing link from 'safety standards met' to 'funding granted.' Trap (B) reverses the conditional; trap (E) is a near-restatement of a premise.
stimulus: Every proposal that is approved by the hospital's research review board meets the federal safety standards. The gene-therapy proposal submitted by Dr. Okafor was approved by the review board last month. It follows that Dr. Okafor's proposal will receive federal funding.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any proposal that meets the federal safety standards will receive federal funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any proposal that receives federal funding meets the federal safety standards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No proposal that fails to meet federal safety standards is approved by the hospital's research review board.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most proposals that meet the federal safety standards receive federal funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Okafor's gene-therapy proposal was approved by the hospital's research review board.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes 'approved → meets safety standards' and applies it to Okafor's proposal, giving us 'Okafor meets safety standards.' The conclusion is 'Okafor receives funding.' The missing link is 'meets safety standards → receives funding,' which (A) supplies as a universal conditional — forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — this gives 'funding → safety,' which doesn't help derive 'funding' from 'safety.'
explanations.C: Restates the first premise in contrapositive form; adds no new bridge to the funding conclusion.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion that Okafor's particular proposal will receive funding.
explanations.E: Restates a premise rather than adding the missing link.

difficultyReason: Two-concept gap between 'fluent in a second language by age seven' and 'capable of native-level pronunciation,' with the conclusion about a specific child. Trap (D) shifts the subject from 'native-level pronunciation' to 'accent-free speech'; trap (C) reverses the key conditional.
stimulus: Linguist: Every child who becomes fluent in a second language by age seven retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in that language throughout life. Mira, who is now an adult, became fluent in Portuguese by age six. So Mira can be trained to speak Portuguese without any detectable foreign accent.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any adult who retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in a language can be trained to speak that language without any detectable foreign accent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adults who became fluent in a second language as children can be trained to speak that language without a foreign accent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every adult who can speak a second language without a detectable foreign accent became fluent in that language before age seven.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any adult who can be trained to speak accent-free in a language retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mira has, in fact, maintained regular exposure to Portuguese since childhood.

explanations.correct: The stimulus gives us 'Mira retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in Portuguese.' The conclusion is 'Mira can be trained to speak without a detectable foreign accent.' (A) supplies the universal bridge from capacity to trainability, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Too weak — 'most' does not guarantee that Mira in particular can be so trained.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional — gives 'accent-free → fluent by seven,' not the direction needed.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — bridges from 'accent-free trainability' back to 'capacity,' not forward.
explanations.E: Adds a factual detail but no logical link between capacity and trainability.

difficultyReason: Two-link chain through 'organic certification' and 'pesticide-free,' with a further jump to 'safe for pregnant consumers.' Trap (E) is a principle-wrapping distractor that sounds strong but trades in different vocabulary.
stimulus: All produce sold at the Harrow Market bears organic certification. Any food that bears organic certification is free of synthetic pesticides. Clearly, then, any produce purchased at the Harrow Market is safe for pregnant consumers to eat.
questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any food that is free of synthetic pesticides is safe for pregnant consumers to eat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any food that is safe for pregnant consumers to eat is free of synthetic pesticides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most foods free of synthetic pesticides are safe for pregnant consumers to eat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some produce sold at the Harrow Market is free of synthetic pesticides.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether a food is safe for pregnant consumers depends principally on the absence of chemical residues of any kind.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'Harrow produce → organic certified → pesticide-free.' The conclusion is 'Harrow produce → safe for pregnant consumers.' (A) adds 'pesticide-free → safe,' closing the final link.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — doesn't help derive safety from the pesticide-free premise.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' does not force the universal conclusion about any produce at the market.
explanations.D: Already entailed by the premises — adds no bridge to safety.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — 'principally' is too weak, and it shifts from pesticides to 'chemical residues of any kind.'

difficultyReason: Counterexample refutation structure modeled on Peacock/Hacker. The critic claims 'publishing under a pseudonym = deceiving readers.' The student must supply the link that someone who cannot deceive readers cannot perform that act. Trap (B) uses 'often' and is too weak.
stimulus: Book critic: Some reviewers have claimed that any novelist who publishes under a pseudonym is deceiving her readers. That is simply wrong. Consider Aleksandra Novak, who publishes her thrillers under the name 'J. R. Larsen' but who discloses her real name openly in every interview and on her publisher's website.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No one who openly discloses her real identity to the public is capable of deceiving her readers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Novelists who use pseudonyms often disclose their real identities in interviews.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any novelist who deceives her readers does so by publishing under a pseudonym.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Readers of thrillers are generally indifferent to whether the author's name is a pseudonym.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pseudonym does not count as a deception unless it is chosen with the intent to deceive.

explanations.correct: The critic needs to show that Novak's using a pseudonym is not deceiving readers. Given that Novak openly discloses her real identity, (A) forces the conclusion: if no one who openly discloses her real identity can deceive her readers, then Novak cannot be deceiving them by using a pseudonym.
explanations.B: Too weak — 'often' and 'disclose in interviews' do not force the conclusion about this author and this act.
explanations.C: Reversed — gives 'deceives → pseudonym,' not 'pseudonym + disclosure → not deceives.'
explanations.D: Reader indifference does not entail that the author is not deceiving them.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping; 'intent to deceive' is a new concept not anchored in the stimulus and does not connect disclosure to non-deception.

difficultyReason: Economic argument with a two-step gap between 'tariff imposed' and 'consumer prices rise,' mediated by 'domestic suppliers raise prices.' Trap (C) supplies a partial bridge; trap (D) is reversed.
stimulus: Whenever a tariff is imposed on an imported good, domestic suppliers of that good raise their own prices. Last month, the government imposed a 20 percent tariff on imported steel. Therefore, consumers will soon pay more for cars manufactured domestically.
questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever domestic suppliers of steel raise their prices, consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars whenever a tariff is imposed on any imported good.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever a tariff is imposed on imported steel, domestic suppliers of steel raise their prices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars, domestic suppliers of steel have raised their prices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic suppliers of steel sometimes raise their prices in response to changes in tariff policy.

explanations.correct: The premises yield 'domestic steel suppliers raise prices.' The conclusion is 'consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars.' (A) provides the universal link from steel-price increases to car-price increases, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Too broad and off-target: it ranges over tariffs on 'any imported good,' not steel specifically, and it bypasses the domestic-supplier mechanism the stimulus uses. (A) supplies the exact link from the step the premises actually establish.
explanations.C: Restates the first premise as applied to steel; adds no bridge to car prices.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'car prices up → steel prices up,' not the needed direction.
explanations.E: Too weak — 'sometimes' cannot force a definite conclusion.

difficultyReason: Environmental-science chain: 'reduce carbon emissions' → 'slow ocean acidification' → 'protect coral reefs.' Student must supply the missing link from acidification to coral protection. Trap (D) inverts the conditional; trap (E) is too weak.
stimulus: Environmentalist: Any policy that significantly reduces global carbon emissions will slow the acidification of the oceans. Our government has just enacted the strictest emissions policy in its history. Therefore, this policy will protect the world's coral reefs from further degradation.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The government's new emissions policy significantly reduces global carbon emissions, and any policy that slows ocean acidification protects the world's coral reefs from further degradation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The government's new emissions policy will not slow ocean acidification unless it also reduces other pollutants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most policies that slow ocean acidification protect some coral reefs from further degradation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any policy that protects the world's coral reefs from further degradation significantly reduces global carbon emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government's emissions policy is likely to contribute, along with other measures, to the protection of coral reefs.

explanations.correct: Two gaps exist: (i) the stimulus says the policy is strict, not that it 'significantly' reduces emissions — the trigger required by the first conditional; and (ii) there is no link from 'slows acidification' to 'protects coral reefs.' (A) supplies both, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Adds a defeater, not a bridge.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' and 'some' do not force a universal conclusion about 'the world's coral reefs.'
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'protects reefs → reduces emissions.'
explanations.E: Too weak — 'likely' and 'along with other measures' do not force the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning chain from 'contract is enforceable' through 'both parties had capacity' to 'agreement is binding.' Trap (B) reverses; trap (C) supplies only a partial bridge.
stimulus: Attorney: A contract is enforceable only if both parties had legal capacity at the time of signing. The agreement between Forsyth Holdings and Vellum Inc. is enforceable, since investigators have confirmed that both signatories had legal capacity. It follows that the agreement is binding on Vellum Inc.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any enforceable contract is binding on each of its parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contract that is binding on its parties is enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any contract whose signatories had legal capacity at the time of signing is enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most enforceable contracts are binding on the corporate parties involved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vellum Inc. signed the agreement under the advice of counsel.

explanations.correct: From the premises, the attorney has established that the contract is enforceable. The conclusion jumps to 'binding on Vellum.' (A) supplies the needed universal link from 'enforceable' to 'binding on each party,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.C: Restates a premise in slightly different terms; adds no link to 'binding.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion about this particular party.
explanations.E: Irrelevant factual detail; does not bridge 'enforceable' to 'binding.'

difficultyReason: Historical-causal structure: the author claims a period could not have been the 'origin of X' because its evidence shows Y. Student must supply the universal principle connecting 'evidence of Y' to 'not origin of X.' Trap (A) shifts the subject; trap (C) is too weak.
stimulus: Historian: Some scholars claim that the early Bronze Age in the Aegean was the origin of complex state bureaucracy. This is mistaken. Recent excavations show that early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies kept no written administrative records whatsoever.
questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No society that lacked writing entirely could have invented any form of bureaucratic practice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No society that kept no written administrative records was the origin of complex state bureaucracy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most societies that developed complex state bureaucracy also developed extensive written administrative records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies maintained oral administrative traditions comparable in sophistication to later written ones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any society that kept written administrative records had complex state bureaucracy.

explanations.correct: The historian establishes that early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies kept no written administrative records. The conclusion is that they were not the origin of complex state bureaucracy. (B) supplies exactly the universal link: 'no written records → not origin,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Shifts the subject from 'origin of complex state bureaucracy' to 'any bureaucratic practice,' and the stimulus did not establish the societies lacked writing entirely — only that they lacked administrative records.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' leaves open that these Aegean societies were the exception.
explanations.D: Weakens the argument by suggesting bureaucracy without writing is possible.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional — gives 'written records → bureaucracy,' not the contrapositive the argument needs.

difficultyReason: Technology/ethics chain: 'algorithm trained on biased data' → 'produces biased predictions' → 'should not be used in hiring.' Trap (D) reverses; trap (A) is a near-restatement of a premise.
stimulus: Data ethicist: Every hiring algorithm trained on historical résumé data inherits the demographic biases present in that data. And any system that inherits demographic biases makes predictions that disadvantage underrepresented applicants. So the algorithm that OmniTrust Corp. plans to deploy in its hiring process ought to be rejected.
questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: OmniTrust Corp.'s algorithm was trained on historical résumé data, and any system that makes predictions disadvantaging underrepresented applicants ought to be rejected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: OmniTrust Corp.'s algorithm has been tested for demographic bias in the past and performed poorly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most algorithms that disadvantage underrepresented applicants ought to be rejected for use in hiring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any algorithm that ought to be rejected disadvantages underrepresented applicants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No hiring algorithm that inherits demographic biases can be corrected through post-deployment auditing.

explanations.correct: Two things are missing: a factual premise placing OmniTrust's algorithm in the class 'trained on historical résumé data,' and the normative bridge from 'disadvantages underrepresented applicants' to 'ought to be rejected.' (A) supplies both, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.B: Adds an empirical claim about past testing, but not the categorical link needed.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion about this particular algorithm.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'ought to be rejected → disadvantages applicants.'
explanations.E: Addresses correctability, not the normative step the argument actually needs.

difficultyReason: Policy argument with a chain from 'passes committee' and 'receives mayor's signature' to 'takes effect before year's end.' Trap (C) reverses the scheduling conditional; trap (E) is a principle-wrapped distractor.
stimulus: Every ordinance that passes the city's zoning committee by October is guaranteed to receive the mayor's signature. The Westbrook rezoning ordinance passed the committee in September. So the Westbrook ordinance will take effect before the end of this year.
questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any ordinance that receives the mayor's signature takes effect before the end of the year in which it is signed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any ordinance that takes effect before the end of a given year has received the mayor's signature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any ordinance that takes effect before the end of a given year passes the city's zoning committee by October.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most ordinances signed by the mayor take effect within a year of their signing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A properly enacted ordinance, once signed, should ordinarily be implemented without undue delay.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that the Westbrook ordinance will receive the mayor's signature this year. The conclusion is that it will take effect before year's end. (A) provides the universal link from signing to year-end effectiveness, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' and 'within a year of signing' do not force that this particular ordinance takes effect before year's end.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping — 'ordinarily' and 'should' do not force the conclusion.
